paras: The attempted lynching of Jack Raymond is an episode in "No Longer a Mystery," a frontier romance credited to the Chicago Herald and reprinted in American newspapers in the autumn of 1888, in which a mob led by the sheriff took Raymond from the jail at San Felipe in the San Joaquin valley to hang him. In the story the noose was already on his neck when the sheriff's own daughter cut him loose and rode off with him. The piece gives no date for the mob and presents itself as a legend told by pioneer settlers, not as a news report.

The story opened with the discovery by two miners of a woman's grave in Sulphur gulch near San Felipe, identified as that of Zarifa Martinique, daughter of Jose Martinique, said to have been sheriff of Fresno county fifteen years earlier. Zarifa refused the rancher Octave Morez, whom her father favored, for Jack Raymond, described as a "shiftless and daring" gambler and prospector. Her father then had Raymond repeatedly jailed on petty charges.

According to the story, a drunken Morez opened fire on Raymond in a saloon, and Raymond shot him through the heart. Raymond fled to the mountains, but the sheriff followed his daughter to their meeting place and, with a posse of citizens, captured him and lodged him in the San Felipe jail.

Although the story says the sheriff knew Raymond had killed in self defense, he spent days in the saloons urging that "the ends of justice" not be cheated. One rainy night a mob, which the writer described as fired by whisky and the sheriff's speeches, went to the jail with a rope, the sheriff at its head. The jailer offered little opposition, and the mob dragged Raymond to a eucalyptus tree on the eastern outskirts of town and threw the rope over a limb.

With the noose on Raymond's neck and a dozen men at the rope, the sheriff began counting to three. Before the count ended, Zarifa galloped into the circle, cut the rope and his bonds, and carried him off toward the mountains while shots were fired after them.

The story says Raymond became the outlaw "Three fingered Jack," killed seven of the men who had tried to lynch him, and was hanged for his crimes at Red Cliff eight years before the feature appeared. No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage.

The only coverage found is this single feature, printed without change as miscellany in the Richmond Daily Times on September 26, 1888, the Wichita Eagle on October 11, the Pawtucket Evening Tribune on October 22 and the Monmouth Inquirer on November 22. It was framed as a "romance" occasioned by the finding of a grave, sympathetic to Raymond and hostile to the sheriff, rather than as news of a lynching attempt. No contemporary news report of a mob at San Felipe, or of Raymond or Morez, was found, and no Black-press coverage exists for this period.

bases: The feature tells of a sheriff-led mob that took Raymond from jail and put a noose on him before he was rescued, an attempted lynching in the story's telling (A2, A3, A5).

In the story, the mob of a dozen or more men led by the sheriff put the noose on Raymond for the killing of Morez, but his rescuer cut the rope and he escaped alive (A2, A3); the account is also an undated romance credited to the Chicago Herald, not a news report (A2, A3).
All coverage is one syndicated feature story, credited to the Chicago Herald and told as a pioneer legend with no date for the mob, reprinted unchanged (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5).

accounts.label: Chicago Herald feature (syndicated)
accounts.gist: A legend told by San Joaquin valley settlers: the sheriff led a whisky-fired mob that took Raymond from jail and put a noose on him, but the sheriff's daughter cut him loose and fled with him.

framing.detail: Printed as a romantic frontier tale under 'No Longer a Mystery', casting Raymond as a sympathetic lover who killed in self defense and the sheriff as acting from spite.
The same text ran as filler fiction in papers in Virginia, Kansas, Rhode Island and New Jersey between September and November 1888.

record_check.dossier: The continuation on the same page has the outcome: the noose was put on Raymond, but the sheriff's daughter cut the rope and he escaped alive; the whole piece is a legend feature, not news.
No date; the story is set years before 1888 (sheriff 'fifteen years ago', Raymond hanged 'eight years ago'); the 1888-10 placement reflects only reprint dates.
Not stated for San Felipe; the sheriff is called sheriff of Fresno county.
Not named in the text; inferred from the San Joaquin valley and Fresno county.
A mob led by the county sheriff, Jose Martinique.
Taken from the jail with little resistance by the jailer, kicked, dragged to a tree, noose placed; shots fired after the escape.

At least four papers, 1888-09-26 to 1888-11-22, all printing the same Chicago Herald feature.

info: Not dated; the story places the sheriff in office 'fifteen years ago' and Raymond's hanging 'eight years ago', counting back from the feature's own time.
San Felipe, in the San Joaquin valley; the mob took Raymond from the San Felipe jail to a eucalyptus tree on the eastern outskirts of the town.
Jack Raymond, later called 'Three fingered Jack'; race not stated.
Accused of killing Octave Morez, whom he shot through the heart in a saloon after Morez, drunk, opened fire on him; the story says the sheriff knew it was self defense.
A mob roused by the sheriff, Jose Martinique, in the saloons of San Felipe and led by him.

The sheriff's daughter, Zarifa Martinique, rode through the crowd, cut the rope and his bonds, and carried Raymond off; he became an outlaw who, the story says, killed seven of the men who had tried to lynch him and was later hanged at Red Cliff.
